partner.persona: a shy apprentice carpenter proud of small progress
partner.topic: reconstructing a grandmother's recipe from an incomplete note
partner.dynamic: The caller and Jun disagree mildly and remain friendly.

messages.content: You're right about the proportions, but I think that little bit of salt she left out on the line was probably just a guess; I'm trying to figure out if it was a specific spice or just her habit. I'm feeling a bit better about it after hearing you're willing to talk, though I still worry I'm overthinking it.

Salt is just salt. It's boring and it's useful.

I used to keep a jar of salt right by the roof tools. When I was fixing a leak, I'd pinch a pinch from the bottle. Sometimes I'd drop a tiny bit on the gutter before nailing the last board. Did she do it? Maybe. Or maybe she just didn't bother.

Most of the time, the salt didn't change anything. It was only a texture. A habit, like brushing your teeth, but without the purpose.

You're right, you don't need to know if it was a specific spice or just a habit. The roof doesn't care, the line doesn't care, and the food doesn't care. The only thing that matters is that you feel better now. If you're overthinking it, then you're just a person in a house, and that's enough.

So, what are we doing now? Fixing the leak? Or just sitting and letting the salt wash away?

Maybe I should just grab that pinch of salt from your roof jar and taste-test it while I measure the new trim? I'd feel much better if I could just make a little something real rather than just sitting here debating the habit.

The salt is right there on the ledge, but I'd rather you didn't.

I'm just a man who likes his roof dry, not a guy who turns his back into a flavor chart. If you grab a pinch, you're going to end up with a mouthful of tears and a headache, and that's a bad way to spend a morning.

Let's just stick to the trim. That's real work. The rest is just noise.
I suppose, I'll just focus on the trim then. I'll try to make sure my joint isn't too tight, though I keep hoping the salted wood will dry faster.

The salt won't stop the wood from drying, and neither will your hope.

Just use a straight piece of wood for your joint. If it's tight, pull back; if it's loose, brace it. That's the only way to keep the roof from leaking later.

I can handle the hammer if you need me. You just hold the wood steady.

I appreciate that, Jun. I'll hold the wood steady while you hammer; it's much more practical than guessing at recipes anyway. I just need to make sure the joint sits flush against the roofline before I tighten the nail.

Got it. Hold the edge tight, and I'll hit the nail in.

Just remember, if the joint sits flush, it stays that way. No amount of salt will fix a loose joint, but a tight one might look okay until the rain starts.

Let's get to it. The sun's getting higher.
Understood, I'll hold the edge tight exactly where you pointed. I'm glad to finally get back to the wood, since thinking about the salt has made my hands feel a bit shaky.

The wood won't shake. Just breathe.

When you're holding it, you don't think about the salt or the dampness. You think only about the pressure on your thumb and the rhythm of my hammer. That's where the work is, not in your head.

Get the edge on the line. I'm ready.
I'll take a deep breath and line up the edge exactly where you said. My thumb feels ready to press down, even if my mind is still a little foggy from all the salt talk.

Okay. Hold the breath for a second.

Your thumb is doing the work, not the fog. If your mind is foggy, that's fine. The wood doesn't care about the fog, only about the gap.

Tap the edge with your knuckle to make sure it's flat against the line. If it wobbles, you'll catch it. If it's steady, then I'll hit.

Ready when you are. Just keep that thumb there.

I'll tap the edge with my knuckle just to feel it settle, then keep my breath steady and my thumb pressed right where we lined it up. You go ahead and hit; I trust your hammer more than my own thoughts.

Good. The wood is quiet now.

I'll drive the nail in. Don't flinch. Just feel the wood vibrate under your thumb.

One, two, three.

There. Now you can feel the weight of it. That's the only thing that matters. The rest can wait.
